tool.name: Linux
tool.tagline: Using and administering Linux systems from the command line
tool.description: Linux is the operating system behind most servers, cloud instances, containers and embedded devices. This curriculum covers working with it from the command line: the filesystem, users and permissions, processes and services, packages, logs, networking and storage, up to the kernel features (namespaces and cgroups) that containers are built on. It is the practical foundation for DevOps, backend and infrastructure work.

glossary.def: The first program Linux starts when the machine switches on; it then starts, watches and stops all the other background programs. Used by most Linux distributions.
To attach a disk (or another file system) at a directory, so its files appear inside Linux's one tree of folders. That directory is the mount point.
A special file under /dev that stands for a piece of hardware, such as a disk; reading or writing it talks to the device.
Regularly starting a fresh log file and renaming, compressing and eventually deleting the old ones, so logs don't fill the disk.
The number Linux uses to identify a user account. Names are just labels for it; root's UID is 0.
The number Linux uses to identify a group of users.
A Linux account meant for a program rather than a person, such as www-data, usually with a UID below 1000 and few rights.
Roughly how many processes were running or waiting to run, averaged over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Compare it with the number of CPU cores.
A process that has finished but whose parent hasn't yet collected its exit status. It uses no CPU or memory, only an entry in the process list.
A download server, run by a Linux distribution or a software maker, that a package manager installs packages from.
The record a Linux file system keeps for each file: its owner, permissions, size, dates and where its data is on the disk. File names point to inodes.
Spare memory Linux fills with copies of files read recently, so reading them again is fast. It's given back to programs as soon as they need it.
Disk space Linux uses as overflow when memory is full. Much slower than real memory, so heavy swapping slows everything down.
An extra name for the same file on a Linux file system. All names are equal; the data is freed only when the last name is removed.
A setting of each process listing the permission bits to take away from new files and directories; 022 gives files rw-r--r-- and directories rwxr-xr-x.
A special permission on a program file: whoever runs it gets the rights of the file's owner (often root) while it runs. passwd uses it.
A special permission: on a directory, new files get the directory's group; on a program, it runs with the file's group.
A special permission on a shared directory, such as /tmp: everyone may create files there, but each user may delete only their own.
Access control list: extra permission rules on a file that give specific users or groups rights beyond owner, group and others.
A small settings file that tells systemd how to run and manage something, such as a background service (name.service) or a timer (name.timer).
One way a machine connects to a network, such as a cable socket, Wi-Fi or a pretend one like lo (localhost). Each has its own IP address.
A machine that passes network traffic between networks; your machine sends packets for other networks to it, usually on their way to the internet.
A machine's list of rules saying where to send packets for each range of IP addresses; the default route covers everything else.
A file made by tar that bundles many files and folders into one, usually compressed, with a name like backup.tar.gz.
A device file for storage, such as a disk or partition (/dev/sda1), read and written in fixed-size blocks.
The file /etc/fstab listing which file systems to mount where each time Linux starts.
The small map at the start of a disk listing its partitions; GPT is the modern format, MBR the old one.
Logical Volume Manager: pools disks into a volume group and cuts resizable logical volumes from it, so storage can grow while in use.
A small extra settings file in a name.d/ directory whose settings are added on top of (and take priority over) the original file, e.g. a systemd unit's.
The small program the firmware starts first; it loads the kernel into memory and starts it with its settings.
A small temporary file system loaded with the kernel at start-up, holding the drivers and tools needed to find and mount the real root file system.
The settings the bootloader passes to the Linux kernel when it starts, such as which disk holds the root file system; shown in /proc/cmdline.
A piece of the Linux kernel, such as a driver, that can be loaded into or removed from the running kernel.
A kernel feature that gives a group of processes their own private copy of one system resource, such as process numbers, network or mounts. Containers are built from them.
Root's powers split into separate pieces (such as 'may open ports below 1024'), so a process can be given only the ones it needs.
A Linux feature that limits which system calls a process may make; container tools use it to block risky ones.
Control group: a Linux kernel feature that puts processes in groups and measures and limits how much CPU, memory, disk and process count each group may use.
In cgroups, the part that measures and limits one resource, such as memory, cpu, io or pids.
A program that keeps starting copies of itself until the machine runs out of processes or memory; a limit on processes stops it.
The Linux kernel feature that lets one program pause and inspect another; debuggers and strace use it.
A Linux feature that runs small, safety-checked programs inside the kernel, used for low-cost watching of what the whole system does.

concepts.name: Kernel, distributions and the shell
concepts.summary: What Linux actually is: the kernel at its core, the programs around it, and the distributions that bundle them together.
concepts.why: Knowing which part of the system you're dealing with tells you where to look for help and fixes.
concepts.body:
Every computer runs an **operating system**: the base software, like Windows or macOS, that starts the machine and lets programs share it. Linux is an operating system too, and it runs most of the world's **servers**: computers that do work for other computers over the network, such as the machines behind websites and apps.

Programs need three main parts of the hardware:

- the **CPU** (processor), the chip that carries out instructions,
- **memory** (RAM), fast short-term storage where running programs keep their data; it empties when the power goes off,
- the **disk**, where files stay for good.

Strictly speaking, Linux is only the **kernel**: the core program that starts first and controls that hardware. It decides which program gets the CPU next, hands out memory, and reads and writes the disk and the network. Ordinary programs can't touch the hardware themselves; they ask the kernel to do it for them. Each such ask is called a **system call**.

What people call "a Linux system" is the kernel plus thousands of ordinary programs: the bash shell you already know, commands like `ls` and `grep`, and **systemd**, the first program to start, which then starts all the others.

A **Linux distribution** (or distro) is a ready-made Linux: kernel, programs, sensible settings and a **package manager**, a tool that installs and updates software for you, like an app store you use from the terminal. The big families:

- **Debian / Ubuntu**: install software with `apt`; very common on servers,
- **Fedora / Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) / Rocky / Alma**: use `dnf`; common in large companies,
- **Arch**, **Alpine** (very small), **SUSE** and others.

These lessons work on all of them; mostly software names and a few file locations differ. The file `/etc/os-release` says which distribution you're on, and `uname -r` which kernel version.

You usually reach a Linux server from your own computer with **SSH**, a secure way to log in to another computer over the network and type commands there. There's no desktop with windows and icons: everything is text, settings live in text files under `/etc`, and almost any task can be scripted. That's why Linux runs most of the **cloud**, the computers companies like Amazon and Google rent out over the internet.
concepts.code:
uname -sr                     # Linux 6.12.0-...   (kernel name and version)
head -n 2 /etc/os-release     # PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS" / NAME="Ubuntu"
hostnamectl                   # computer name, operating system, kernel, chip type
uptime                        # up 3 days, ...   (time since the machine started)
whoami                        # ada   (the account you are logged in as)
echo "$SHELL"                 # /bin/bash
nproc                         # 4   (CPU cores: instructions it can run at the same moment)
free -h | head -n 2           # memory: total / used / available
takeaways: Linux is the kernel; a distribution adds programs, a package manager and defaults
Debian/Ubuntu use apt, Fedora/RHEL use dnf
/etc/os-release and uname -r identify the system
pitfalls: Searching for help without saying which distribution you run; software names and file locations differ.

quiz.q: What does the Linux kernel itself do?
options: Shares the CPU, memory and devices between programs
quiz.explain: The kernel controls the hardware; shells, package managers and desktops are ordinary programs that run on top of it.

quiz.q: Which file tells you the distribution and its version?
quiz.explain: /etc/os-release is the standard file describing the distribution, in a form both people and scripts can read.

concepts.name: The filesystem hierarchy
concepts.summary: One tree of folders starting at /: what lives in /etc, /var, /home, /usr, /tmp, /proc and /dev.
concepts.why: Knowing the standard layout means you can find any settings file or log on a machine you've never seen.
concepts.body:
On Windows each drive gets a letter, like `C:`. Linux instead has one single tree of folders starting at `/`, called the root. Linux people say **directory** for folder; the two words mean the same. Every file has a path from `/`, such as `/home/ada/notes.txt`.

Extra disks and USB sticks don't get letters either. They are **mounted**: attached at some directory, so their files appear inside the one tree. The way a disk's space is organised into files and folders is called a **file system**, and each mounted disk is also called a file system.

The main directories follow a standard layout, so every Linux machine looks alike:

- `/etc`: settings for the whole system, as **configuration files** (text files you can read and edit),
- `/home/<user>`: each person's own files; `/root` is the home of root, the administrator (more in the users lesson),
- `/usr`: installed programs (`/usr/bin`) and the shared code they use (`/usr/lib`); `/usr/local` for software you install by hand,
- `/opt`: big add-on applications that keep everything in one folder,
- `/tmp`: temporary files, often wiped when the machine restarts,
- `/boot`: the kernel and the files needed to start the machine,
- `/mnt` and `/media`: where extra or removable disks usually get mounted.

`/var` holds data that changes while the system runs. The most important part is `/var/log`, full of **log files**: running programs write a dated line there for each thing they do, so you can find out later what happened.

Some directories don't hold real files at all. In `/dev`, each piece of hardware, such as a disk, appears as a **device file**; the `/dev/null` you met in bash is one. `/proc` and `/sys` are made up on the spot by the kernel: reading `/proc/loadavg` asks the kernel a question, and the answer comes back as text. `/run` holds small notes running programs leave for each other, and is emptied at every start.

This is the old Unix idea that "everything is a file": disks, running programs and kernel settings are all read and written with the same file tools you already know.
concepts.code:
ls /
# bin boot dev etc home lib media mnt opt proc root run srv sys tmp usr var
ls -ld /bin                 # lrwxrwxrwx ... /bin -> usr/bin   (just a shortcut to /usr/bin)
ls /etc | head -n 3         # system-wide settings files
ls /var/log | head -n 3     # log files
cat /proc/loadavg           # kernel information presented as a file
ls -l /dev/null             # crw-rw-rw- ... /dev/null   (c at the start: a device)
echo ~ "$HOME"              # /home/ada /home/ada
takeaways: One tree from /; other disks are mounted into it
Settings in /etc, logs and changing data in /var, programs in /usr
/proc, /sys and /dev show the kernel and hardware as files
pitfalls: Keeping files you need in /tmp, which may be wiped when the machine restarts.

quiz.q: Where would you look first for a program's log files?
quiz.explain: Data that changes while the system runs lives under /var, and logs by convention in /var/log.

quiz.q: What is special about /proc?
options: Its files are made up on the spot by the kernel
quiz.explain: Nothing in /proc is stored on disk; the kernel produces each file's content when you read it, to show information about running programs and the system.

concepts.name: Navigating and managing files
concepts.summary: Move around with cd and ls, and create, copy, move, find and delete files and directories.
concepts.why: These dozen commands are what you type most on any Linux machine.
concepts.body:
A path that starts with `/` is an **absolute path**: the full address from the top of the tree, which means the same thing wherever you are. Any other path is a **relative path**, read starting from the directory you're in right now.

That current directory is your **working directory**. `.` means the working directory itself, `..` the directory above it, and `~` your home. `pwd` (print working directory) shows where you are, `cd dir` moves into a directory, `cd` alone goes home, and `cd -` jumps back to where you were before.

`ls` lists a directory. `-l` gives the long format (permissions, owner, size, date), `-h` shows sizes in readable units like `4.0K`, and `-t` sorts newest first. `-a` also shows **hidden files**, whose names start with a dot; they usually hold settings.

Names are **case-sensitive**: `Notes.txt` and `notes.txt` are two different files. Endings like `.txt` are only a naming habit; Linux doesn't use them to decide what a file is.

Managing files:

- `mkdir -p a/b/c` creates directories, including any missing ones on the way; `touch f` creates an empty file,
- `cp src dst` copies; add `-r` to copy a directory with everything inside it, however deep, or `-a` to also keep permissions and dates,
- `mv src dst` moves **or renames**,
- `rm f` deletes a file, `rm -r dir` a directory and everything in it, and `rmdir` an empty directory.

There is **no trash can**: `rm` is permanent. Use `-i` to be asked first, check what a pattern like `*.log` matches with `ls` before deleting, and never run `rm -rf` with a variable that might be empty.

`find` searches a whole tree by name, type, size or age: `find . -name '*.log' -mtime +7` lists `.log` files last changed more than 7 days ago; add `-delete` or `-exec` to act on them. `tree` (if installed) draws a directory and everything below it.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"                # make a fresh temporary directory and go into it
pwd                              # /tmp/tmp.Xyz
mkdir -p project/src/utils       # -p: create missing parents, no error if present
touch project/README.md
cp project/README.md project/README.bak
mv project/README.bak project/notes.md   # move = rename
ls -la project                   # long listing, hidden files included
cp -r project project-copy       # -r for directories
rm -r project-copy               # delete it all: there is no undo
find . -name '*.md' | sort       # ./project/README.md ./project/notes.md
find . -type d -empty            # ./project/src/utils   (empty directories)
cd project/src && cd ../..       # .. is the directory above
cd - >/dev/null && pwd           # back to the previous directory
takeaways: Absolute paths start with /; . is here, .. is the directory above, ~ is home
cp -r and rm -r for directories; mv also renames
rm is permanent; find searches by name, type, size and age
pitfalls: Running `rm -rf "$DIR"/*` when DIR is empty: it expands to /*, every file on the machine.

quiz.q: What does `mv report.txt final.txt` do in the same directory?
options: Fails because final.txt does not exist
Moves it to a directory named final.txt only
quiz.explain: mv to a new name in the same directory is a rename.

quiz.q: Which command lists files under the current directory with names ending in .log?
quiz.explain: find looks through every directory below the starting point, and -name matches a pattern against each file name.

concepts.name: Viewing files and searching text
concepts.summary: Read files with cat, less, head and tail, follow logs live and search them with grep.
concepts.why: Reading settings files and logs is most of what fixing a server looks like.
concepts.body:
Choose the viewer by file size and purpose:

- `cat file` prints a small file in one go,
- `less file` pages through anything, however large: Space and b to move, `/text` to search, `n` for the next match, `G` for the end, `q` to quit,
- `head -n 20` and `tail -n 20` show the beginning or the end,
- `tail -f app.log` **follows** a file, printing new lines as they're written.

Programs regularly start a fresh log file and rename the old one, so logs don't grow forever; this is called **log rotation**. `tail -F` (capital F) keeps following the new file when that happens.

`grep pattern files` prints the lines that match. Common options: `-i` ignore upper/lower case, `-n` show line numbers, `-r` search every file under a directory, `-v` invert (lines that do **not** match), `-c` count, `-l` only file names, `-E` use the fuller regular expression language, `-C 3` show three lines around each match. Combine them with pipes: `grep -v '^#' sshd_config | grep -v '^$'` shows the SSH settings file without comment lines and blank lines.

`wc -l` counts lines, `file` tells you what a file actually contains (text, a program, an archive...), and `diff a b` compares two files line by line.

Old logs are often stored **compressed**: squeezed to take less space, with names ending in `.gz`. `zcat`, `zless` and `zgrep` read them without unpacking first.

Don't `cat` a program file or a huge log into the terminal: a program isn't text and fills the screen with garbage. Use `less` or `head`. "Permission denied" means your account isn't allowed to read the file; often a command run as the administrator, like `sudo less file`, gets you in (see the users lesson).
concepts.code:
cat /etc/hostname                 # print a small file
less /var/log/syslog              # page: / search, n next, G end, q quit
head -n 3 /etc/passwd             # first 3 lines
tail -n 20 /var/log/nginx/error.log
tail -F /var/log/nginx/access.log # follow new lines, even after rotation
wc -l /etc/passwd                 # 32 /etc/passwd
grep -n '^root' /etc/passwd       # 1:root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
grep -ri 'timeout' /etc/nginx/    # every file below, ignoring case
grep -v '^#' /etc/ssh/sshd_config | grep -v '^$'   # settings without comments
grep -c ' 500 ' access.log        # count lines with status 500 (server errors)
zgrep 'error' /var/log/syslog.2.gz   # search a compressed log
file /usr/bin/ls                  # ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable ...  (a program)
takeaways: less for big files, head/tail for ends, tail -f to follow
grep -i -n -r -v -c cover most searches
zcat, zless and zgrep read compressed logs
pitfalls: Opening a huge log file with cat or a text editor instead of less or tail.

quiz.q: Which command shows new log lines as they are written?
quiz.explain: tail -f keeps the file open and prints appended lines.

quiz.q: What does `grep -v '^#' file` output?
quiz.explain: -v inverts the match, so comment lines are filtered out.

concepts.name: Users, groups and root
concepts.summary: How Linux tells users and groups apart, what root is, and how sudo grants administrator rights safely.
concepts.why: Every 'Permission denied', every time sudo asks for a password, and every program's rights come down to users and groups.
concepts.body:
Linux was built for many people sharing one machine, so it always knows who is doing what. Each person has a user account, and every program runs as some user. Inside, the system knows users by a number, the **UID** (user ID); the name is just a label for it.

Users belong to **groups**: named sets of users who can be given access together, such as everyone allowed to look after the machine. Each user has one main group and can be in more. Groups have numbers too, the **GID**. `id` shows your UID, GID and groups; `whoami` just your name.

Accounts are defined in text files under `/etc`:

- `/etc/passwd`: one line per user, `name:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell` (despite the name, no passwords),
- `/etc/shadow`: the passwords, stored as **hashes**, scrambled fingerprints from which the password can't be read back; only root may read this file,
- `/etc/group`: groups and their members.

`getent passwd name` and `getent group name` look an account up, including accounts kept on a central company server rather than in these files.

**root** (UID 0) is the **superuser**, the administrator account. It skips every permission check and can do anything, including wreck the system with one typo. So you don't work as root.

Instead you use **sudo** ("superuser do") to run a single command as root: `sudo apt update`. sudo asks for **your own** password, not root's. It checks the rules in `/etc/sudoers` (often "members of the `sudo` or `wheel` group may run anything") and records every command. `sudo -i` opens a root shell when you need many commands; `su - user` switches to another user, with that user's password.

Besides people, there are **system users** (UIDs below 1000) such as `www-data`, `postgres` or `nobody`. Programs that run all the time in the background, like the software behind a website, each run as their own system user with few rights. If an attacker takes one over, they can't take over the whole machine.
concepts.code:
whoami                     # ada
id                         # uid=1000(ada) gid=1000(ada) groups=1000(ada),27(sudo),998(docker)
grep '^ada:' /etc/passwd   # ada:x:1000:1000:Ada,,,:/home/ada:/bin/bash
getent group sudo          # sudo:x:27:ada   (ada is in the sudo group)
getent passwd www-data     # www-data:x:33:33:...:/var/www:/usr/sbin/nologin   (a system user)
sudo -l                    # which commands may I run with sudo?
sudo apt update            # one command as root (asks for YOUR password)
sudo -i                    # a root shell; type exit to leave
su - bob                   # become bob (needs bob's password)
takeaways: Users and groups are numbers (UID/GID); root is UID 0
/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and /etc/group define accounts
Use sudo for single admin commands rather than working as root
pitfalls: Working as root all the time, so one typo or one hijacked script can destroy the system.

quiz.q: Whose password does `sudo` ask for by default?
quiz.explain: sudo checks that it's really you, then looks in /etc/sudoers to see what you may run.

quiz.q: Why does a website's server program run as the system user www-data instead of root?
options: To limit the damage if an attacker takes it over
quiz.explain: If an attacker takes over the program, they only get www-data's few rights, not the whole machine.

concepts.name: File permissions: chmod and chown
concepts.summary: Read rwx permission strings, change them with symbolic and octal chmod, and change ownership with chown.
concepts.why: Permission errors are the most common Linux problem, and wrong permissions are a common way attackers get in.
concepts.body:
Every file has an **owner** (a user) and a group, and three sets of permissions: one for the owner, one for members of the group, and one for everybody else, called "others". Together these are the file's **file permissions**.

`ls -l` shows them as a string like `-rwxr-x---`. The first character is the type: `-` a file, `d` a directory, `l` a link (a shortcut to another file). Then come three `rwx` sets: owner, group, others. A dash means that permission is missing.

For **files**, `r` allows reading, `w` changing, and `x` running it as a program or script. For **directories** the meaning differs: `r` lets you list the names inside, `w` lets you create, delete and rename files in it, and `x` lets you go into it and use the files inside. A directory usually needs `r` and `x` together.

`chmod` changes permissions, written in one of two ways:

- with letters: `u`, `g`, `o` (user, group, others), then `+` to add, `-` to remove or `=` to set exactly: `chmod u+x script.sh`, `chmod go-w file`, `chmod u=rw,g=r,o= file`,
- with numbers: each set becomes one digit by adding r=4, w=2, x=1. So 6 is `rw-`, 5 is `r-x`, and `chmod 644` means `rw-r--r--`, `755` means `rwxr-xr-x`, `600` means `rw-------`.

`chown user:group file` changes the owner and group (only root may do this); `chgrp` changes just the group. `-R` changes a whole directory and everything inside it; use it with care, because making a whole tree runnable or writable by everybody is a classic mistake.

Typical settings: scripts `755`; settings files that contain passwords `640`, owned by root and readable by the program's group; website files readable, but not writable, by the website program's user.

SSH logins can use a pair of keys instead of a password: a **private key** that never leaves your computer, and a public one you copy to the server. Keep the private key at `600`: SSH refuses to use one that other users could read.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"                # a fresh temporary directory
touch script.sh notes.txt
ls -l script.sh                  # -rw-r--r-- 1 ada ada 0 ... script.sh
chmod +x script.sh               # add x: now it can be run
chmod u=rwx,g=rx,o= script.sh
stat -c '%A %a %n' script.sh     # -rwxr-x--- 750 script.sh   (letters and number)
chmod 640 notes.txt
stat -c '%A %a %n' notes.txt     # -rw-r----- 640 notes.txt
mkdir shared && chmod 750 shared # dirs: x = may enter, r = may list
stat -c '%A %a %n' shared        # drwxr-x--- 750 shared
# sudo chown ada:developers notes.txt     # owner and group
# sudo chown -R www-data: /var/www/site   # whole tree; "user:" = that user's main group
takeaways: rwx for owner, group and others; as numbers r=4 w=2 x=1
On directories x means enter, r means list, w means create/delete
chown user:group changes ownership; be careful with -R
pitfalls: Fixing a permission error with chmod 777, which lets every user change (or replace) the file.

quiz.q: What does chmod 640 give a file?
A user can list a directory's names but gets 'Permission denied' opening any file inside. Which bit is missing on the directory?
options: The directory must be owned by root
quiz.explain: x on a directory is needed to use the files inside it; r only lets you list their names.

concepts.name: Processes: ps, top and friends
concepts.summary: Every running program is a process with an ID number and a parent; list and watch them with ps, top and pgrep.
concepts.why: Finding what's running, what's using up the CPU or memory and what started what is everyday Linux work.
concepts.body:
You met processes in bash: a **process** is one running copy of a program. Open three terminals and you have three bash processes. The kernel gives each one a number, its **process ID** (PID), plus its own memory and an owner, the user it runs as.

Every process is started by another one, its parent, whose PID is called the **PPID**. So processes form a family tree. At the top is PID 1, systemd, which the kernel starts first and which starts everything else. In bash, `$$` is the shell's own PID.

Listing processes:

- `ps` alone shows the processes in your terminal; `ps aux` or `ps -ef` (two older spellings that do the same job) show all of them,
- `ps -o pid,ppid,user,%cpu,%mem,stat,etime,cmd` picks exactly what to show,
- `ps -ef --forest` or `pstree` draw the family tree,
- `pgrep -a name` finds PIDs by name, `pidof prog` by exact program name.

`top` (or the friendlier `htop`) shows a live view with the busiest processes first. In top, press `M` to sort by memory, `P` by CPU, `k` to stop a process and `q` to quit.

The top lines show how long the machine has been running, the number of processes, memory use and the **load average**: roughly how many processes wanted the CPU, averaged over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. A CPU with 4 cores can run 4 things at the same moment, so on such a machine a load around 4 means it's fully busy.

The `STAT` letter shows each process's state:

- `R` running, or ready to run,
- `S` sleeping: waiting for something such as a keypress or data; the normal state,
- `D` waiting on the disk or network storage, and can't be interrupted until it answers,
- `T` stopped (paused),
- `Z` **zombie**: finished, but its parent hasn't yet collected its exit status.

A few zombies are harmless. A growing number means the parent program has a **bug**, a mistake in its code.
concepts.code:
echo $$                               # PID of this shell
ps                                    # processes of this terminal
ps aux | head -n 3                    # USER PID %CPU %MEM VSZ RSS TTY STAT START TIME COMMAND
ps -ef --forest | tail -n 5           # parent/child tree
ps -o pid,ppid,stat,etime,cmd -p $$   # chosen details for one PID
pgrep -a sshd                         # PIDs and full commands, found by name
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -n 5       # the biggest memory users
top                                   # live view: M memory, P CPU, q quit
takeaways: Each process has a PID, a parent and an owner; PID 1 is systemd
ps aux / ps -ef list everything; pgrep finds by name
STAT: R running, S sleeping, D waiting on disk, Z zombie
pitfalls: Reading `ps aux | grep nginx` and counting the grep process itself as a match; use pgrep.

quiz.q: What does a process in state D usually indicate?
options: It's waiting on the disk or network storage and can't be interrupted
It is running in the background
quiz.explain: D means it's waiting for storage to answer; it can't even be stopped until the disk responds.

quiz.q: Which process is the ancestor of all others on a typical modern distribution?
quiz.explain: The kernel starts PID 1, usually systemd, which starts everything else.

concepts.name: Signals and stopping processes
concepts.summary: Ask processes to stop or reload with signals: SIGTERM, SIGKILL, SIGINT, SIGHUP, SIGSTOP and SIGCONT.
concepts.why: Stopping a stuck program correctly, without losing data, depends on picking the right signal.
concepts.body:
How do you ask a running program to stop? You send it a **signal**: a short notice, delivered by the kernel, that interrupts whatever the program is doing. Each signal has a name and a number.

A program can **handle** most signals (run its own code first, for example to save its work), **ignore** them, or let the default happen, which is usually to end. The ones to know:

- `SIGTERM` (15): "please finish up and exit". It's what `kill` sends unless told otherwise; well-behaved programs save their work and exit. Linux sends it first when it shuts a program down.
- `SIGINT` (2): what Ctrl-C sends to the program running in your terminal.
- `SIGKILL` (9): ends the process at once. It **can't be handled**, so nothing gets tidied up: temporary files and half-written data may be left behind. Use it only when SIGTERM fails.
- `SIGHUP` (1): originally "the terminal hung up". Many long-running programs, such as nginx (which serves websites), reread their settings when they get it.
- `SIGSTOP` / `SIGCONT`: pause and resume. Ctrl-Z sends `SIGTSTP`, a pause the program is allowed to handle.

Send them with `kill -SIGNAL PID` (`kill -TERM 1234`, `kill -9 1234`), by name with `pkill pattern` or `killall name`; `kill -l` lists them all. You can only signal your own processes, unless you are root.

The usual order: `kill PID`, wait a few seconds, check with `ps`, and only then `kill -9`. A process in state `D` (waiting on the disk) or a zombie won't go away with any signal: fix the disk problem, or the parent.
concepts.code:
sleep 600 &                          # & runs it in the background; the terminal stays free
pid=$!                               # $! = PID of that background command
kill "$pid"                          # SIGTERM (15): please exit
sleep 600 & pid=$!
kill -STOP "$pid"                    # pause it
ps -o pid,stat,cmd -p "$pid"         # STAT T = stopped
kill -CONT "$pid"                    # resume
kill -9 "$pid"                       # SIGKILL: no tidying up, last resort
kill -l | head -n 2                  # signal numbers and names
pkill -f 'python worker.py'          # match against whole command lines
sudo kill -HUP 1234                  # as root: tell process 1234 (say, nginx) to reread its settings
sudo systemctl kill -s HUP nginx     # the same through systemd (services lesson)
takeaways: kill sends SIGTERM by default: ask first
SIGKILL (9) cannot be handled; use it last
SIGHUP often means 'reload configuration'
pitfalls: Reaching for kill -9 first, which takes away the program's chance to save its data and tidy up.

quiz.q: Which signal can a program NOT catch or ignore?
quiz.explain: SIGKILL (and SIGSTOP) are carried out by the kernel itself; the process gets no chance to react.

quiz.q: What does Ctrl-C send to the foreground process?
quiz.explain: The terminal turns Ctrl-C into SIGINT for the program running in it.

concepts.name: Installing software with package managers
concepts.summary: Install, update, search and remove software with apt on Debian/Ubuntu and dnf on Fedora/RHEL.
concepts.why: A package manager installs software together with everything it needs, and keeps it updated with security fixes; hand-installed software goes stale.
concepts.body:
On a phone you install apps from an app store. Linux had that idea first. A distribution ships its software as **packages**: ready-to-install bundles of a program and its files. They come from **package repositories**, download servers that the distribution runs and signs, so you can tell the packages are genuine.

Most programs need other packages to work, called their **dependencies**. The package manager works these out and installs them too. It also records which package each file came from, and later upgrades everything together, including security fixes. That's why the first answer to "how do I install X?" should be the package manager. Installing needs root, so those commands start with `sudo`.

On **Debian and Ubuntu** (`apt`, `.deb` files):

- `sudo apt update` refreshes the list of available packages (do this first),
- `sudo apt install pkg`, `sudo apt remove pkg` (`purge` also deletes its settings), `sudo apt upgrade`,
- `apt search term`, `apt show pkg`; `dpkg -L pkg` lists a package's files and `dpkg -S /path` says which package a file came from.

On **Fedora, RHEL, Rocky and Alma** (`dnf`, `.rpm` files): `sudo dnf install pkg`, `dnf remove`, `dnf upgrade`, `dnf search`, `dnf provides /usr/bin/dig` and `rpm -ql pkg`. Others: `pacman -S` on Arch, `apk add` on Alpine, `zypper` on SUSE.

Extra package repositories, such as the ones Docker or PostgreSQL publish for their own software, add programs your distribution doesn't carry. Only add ones you trust: packages install as root. **Snap** and **Flatpak** are separate formats that bundle each app with everything it needs, mostly for desktop apps.

Python and other languages have their own package managers too, such as `pip` and `npm`. Don't run them with `sudo` to install into the system's own directories: you can break tools the system relies on. Install per user, or into a **virtual environment**, a private folder of packages for one project.
concepts.code:
# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt update                  # refresh the package lists first
sudo apt install -y htop         # install, with its dependencies (-y: don't ask)
apt search ripgrep               # find packages
apt show nginx | head -n 5       # version, size, description
sudo apt upgrade                 # update everything installed
sudo apt remove htop             # purge would also delete its settings
dpkg -L curl | head -n 3         # files installed by a package
dpkg -S /usr/bin/ssh             # openssh-client: /usr/bin/ssh
# Fedora / RHEL
sudo dnf install htop
dnf provides /usr/bin/dig        # which package ships a file
# Arch: sudo pacman -S htop     Alpine: apk add htop
takeaways: apt update before apt install; dnf on Fedora/RHEL
dpkg -S / dnf provides find which package a file belongs to
Prefer your distribution's packages; add only package repositories you trust
pitfalls: Running `sudo pip install` into the system's own Python and breaking system tools that use it.

quiz.q: On Ubuntu, `apt install foo` says 'Unable to locate package' for a package that exists. What should you try first?
quiz.explain: The local list of packages may be out of date or empty, for example on a freshly created machine.

quiz.q: How do you find which package provides /usr/bin/dig on Fedora?
quiz.explain: dnf provides searches package file lists for the given path.

concepts.name: Disk and memory usage: df, du, free
concepts.summary: See how full each disk is with df, find what uses the space with du, and read memory use correctly with free.
concepts.why: Full disks and memory running out are among the most common reasons servers break.
concepts.body:
Sizes are counted in **bytes**; one byte holds about one letter of text. A **gigabyte** (`G`) is about a billion bytes, a megabyte (`M`) a million.

`df -h` ("disk free") shows each mounted file system with its size, used and available space in those readable units. `df -h /var` shows just the one that holds `/var`.

A file system also keeps one small record per file, called an **inode**, and it has a fixed number of them. With millions of tiny files it can run out of inodes while space is still free; `df -i` checks.

`du` measures what directories contain: `du -sh dir` gives one total, and `du -h --max-depth=1 /var | sort -h` lists the directories inside by size, so you can dig down step by step. `ncdu` is an interactive version.

If `df` says the disk is full but `du` can't find what's using it, a program may still have a **deleted** file open, often an old log. Linux frees a deleted file's space only when the last program using it closes it. `lsof +L1` lists such files, and restarting that program frees the space.

`free -h` shows memory. Linux deliberately fills spare memory with copies of files it read recently, the **page cache**, so reading them again is quick. So "free" is often small on a healthy machine. The number that matters is **available**: memory programs can get, including page cache that can be dropped.

**Swap** is disk space used as overflow when memory is full. A little swap use is fine, but constant swapping makes everything slow, because the disk is far slower than memory.

On servers, watch `/var`: logs, app data and Docker's downloads (`/var/lib/docker`) all grow there. Set up automatic cleanup of old logs and an alert before the disk fills.
concepts.code:
df -h                          # size, used, available per mounted file system
df -h /var                     # only the file system holding /var
df -i /                        # inodes: "No space left" though space looks free?
du -sh ~/Downloads             # total size of one directory
sudo du -h --max-depth=1 /var 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -n 5   # biggest directories
sudo lsof +L1                  # deleted files still held open
free -h
#        total   used   free  shared  buff/cache  available
# Mem:    15Gi  4.1Gi  1.0Gi   0.5Gi        10Gi       10Gi
# Swap:  2.0Gi     0B  2.0Gi
takeaways: df shows free space per filesystem, du shows what uses it
df -i for inodes; lsof +L1 for deleted-but-open files
In free, read 'available', not 'free'
pitfalls: Panicking because `free` shows little free memory, when most of it is page cache the system can drop.

quiz.q: df says the disk is 100% full but du on / totals much less. A likely cause?
options: A process holds a deleted file open
quiz.explain: Space of a deleted file is freed only when the last process closes it; lsof +L1 finds them.

quiz.q: Which column of `free -h` best tells you how much memory new programs can use?
quiz.explain: available counts the page cache the kernel can hand to programs when they need it.

concepts.name: Inodes, hard links and symlinks
concepts.summary: How files really work: an inode holds a file's data and details, names are links to it, and symlinks store a path.
concepts.why: Links explain switching app versions with a 'current' symlink, why deleting a file may not free space, and how many tools behave.
concepts.body:
In the disk lesson you met the **inode**, the record a file system keeps for each file. It holds the file's **metadata** (data about the file: owner, permissions, size, and when it was created and last changed) and where its contents sit on the disk. The file's name is not in the inode. A directory is just a list that pairs names with inode numbers. `ls -i` shows the numbers and `stat` the full metadata.

A **hard link** (`ln target name`) adds another name for the same inode. Both names are equal; there is no "original". The inode keeps a **link count**, and the data is freed only when the count reaches zero **and** no process still has the file open. Hard links can't cross from one file system to another and can't point to directories.

A **symbolic link**, or symlink (`ln -s target name`), is a small special file that contains a **path**. Opening it follows the path, like a shortcut on a desktop. Symlinks can point anywhere, including directories and other file systems, but if the target is moved or deleted the link **dangles**: it points at nothing. A relative target is read starting from the link's own directory, not from where you ran `ln`.

Useful commands: `readlink link` prints the stored path, `readlink -f` the final, fully followed one; `ls -l` shows `name -> target`; `find -L` follows links, `find -type l` finds them.

A common way to release a new version of an app: install each version in its own directory and point a `current` symlink at the one in use, with `ln -sfn /opt/app-2.1 /opt/app/current`. The switch is **atomic**: anyone opening `current` gets either the old version or the new one, never a half-switched mix. Going back to the previous version, a **rollback**, is just as instant.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
echo "hello" > original.txt
ln original.txt hard.txt          # hard link: another name, same inode
ln -s original.txt soft.txt       # symlink: a file containing a path
ls -li | sort -k10
# 1234 -rw-r--r-- 2 ada ada  6 ... hard.txt
# 1234 -rw-r--r-- 2 ada ada  6 ... original.txt
# 1240 lrwxrwxrwx 1 ada ada 12 ... soft.txt -> original.txt
rm original.txt
cat hard.txt                      # hello  (data lives while a link remains)
cat soft.txt                      # cat: soft.txt: No such file or directory
readlink soft.txt                 # original.txt  (the dangling path)
stat -c '%h links: %n' hard.txt   # 1 links: hard.txt
mkdir app-2.0 app-2.1
ln -sfn app-2.1 current && readlink current   # app-2.1  (switch a release)
takeaways: An inode holds a file's data and metadata; names are links to it
Hard links share an inode; symlinks store a path and can dangle
ln -sfn switches a 'current' symlink atomically
pitfalls: Creating a relative symlink from another directory and expecting the path to be relative to where you ran ln.

quiz.q: After `ln a.txt b.txt; rm a.txt`, what happens to b.txt?
options: It still has the full content
quiz.explain: Both names pointed to the same inode; removing one name leaves the data reachable through the other.

quiz.q: Which can point to a directory on another filesystem?
quiz.explain: Symlinks store a path, so they can point anywhere; hard links stay within one file system and can't point at directories.

concepts.name: umask, setuid, setgid and sticky bit
concepts.summary: Default permissions via umask, and the special bits that make passwd work, shared group folders and a safe /tmp.
concepts.why: These bits explain permissions you will see on real systems and are essential for shared directories and security audits.
concepts.body:
New files start from mode 666 (`rw-rw-rw-`) and directories from 777, minus the bits in your **umask**. The common umask `022` removes write for group and others, giving `644` files and `755` directories; `077` makes everything private. Set it in `~/.bashrc`, the file of commands bash runs each time it starts.

Three special bits form an extra digit in front of the usual three:

- **setuid** (4000, `s` in the owner's set): a program runs with its **owner's** rights instead of yours. `/usr/bin/passwd` is setuid root, so ordinary users can change their password in `/etc/shadow`. Setuid programs are favourite targets for attackers; list them with `find / -perm -4000`.
- **setgid** (2000, `s` in the group's set): on a **directory**, new files get the directory's group instead of their creator's main group, which is ideal for team folders. On a program, it runs with the file's group.
- **sticky bit** (1000, `t` in the others' set): on a directory, users may delete only their **own** files, even though everybody may write there. That's why `/tmp` is `1777`.

A capital `S` or `T` means the special bit is set without the `x` underneath it.

When owner, group and others aren't enough, **ACLs** (access control lists) give rights to extra users and groups: `setfacl -m u:bob:rw file`, read back with `getfacl`. A `+` after the permission string in `ls -l` marks a file that has an ACL.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
umask                            # 0022 -> new files 644, directories 755
(umask 077; touch private.txt; stat -c '%a %n' private.txt)   # 600 private.txt
ls -l /usr/bin/passwd            # -rwsr-xr-x 1 root root ...  (setuid root)
ls -ld /tmp                      # drwxrwxrwt ...  (sticky)
mkdir team && chmod 2775 team
stat -c '%A %a' team             # drwxrwsr-x 2775  (setgid directory)
chmod +t team && stat -c '%a' team   # 3775
find /usr/bin -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null | head -n 3   # setuid binaries
# sudo setfacl -m u:bob:rw report.txt && getfacl report.txt  # per-user ACL
takeaways: umask subtracts bits from 666/777 for new files and directories
setuid runs as the file owner; setgid dirs share a group; sticky protects others' files
ACLs grant extra users or groups access
pitfalls: Setting setuid on a script, or on a program that runs scripts (like bash or python): then any user can run any code with the owner's rights, often root's.

quiz.q: Why is /tmp mode 1777?
options: Everyone can create files, but only owners can delete their own
So only root can write there
New files inherit the tmp group
quiz.explain: The sticky bit (1) on a world-writable directory protects each user's files from others.

quiz.q: With umask 027, what mode does a new regular file get?
quiz.explain: 666 with group write and all 'other' bits removed gives 640.

concepts.name: Managing users and sudo rules
concepts.summary: Create and modify users and groups, grant sudo rights in small files under /etc/sudoers.d, and lock or remove accounts.
concepts.why: Adding people, creating accounts for programs and limiting admin rights are routine server tasks.
concepts.body:
The basic tools work on every distribution:

- `useradd -m -s /bin/bash name` creates a user with a home directory and bash as their shell (Debian's friendlier `adduser` asks questions instead),
- `passwd name` sets a password, `passwd -l name` locks it,
- `usermod -aG group name` **adds** the user to another group. Without `-a`, `-G` replaces all their extra groups: a classic way to take away someone's sudo rights by accident,
- `groupadd`, `gpasswd -d user group` (remove from a group), `userdel -r name` (also deletes the home directory).

Group changes take effect when the user next logs in (or with `newgrp group` in a single shell), because a user's groups are fixed at the moment they log in.

Accounts for programs, called **service accounts**, are system users that can't log in: their shell is `/usr/sbin/nologin`, a program that just refuses. Create one with `useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin myapp`.

**sudo rules** live in `/etc/sudoers`. Never edit it directly: `visudo` checks the file for mistakes before saving, because a broken sudoers file can lock everyone out of root. Better still, put rules in small files in `/etc/sudoers.d/`, edited with `visudo -f`. A rule reads `who where=(as_whom) what`. For scripts and automated jobs, allow exact commands, optionally with `NOPASSWD`, rather than `ALL`. For people, the norm is logging in with an SSH key and then using sudo, with direct root login over SSH switched off.
concepts.code:
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -c "Bob Builder" bob   # -m creates /home/bob
sudo passwd bob                    # set a password
sudo usermod -aG developers bob    # ADD to a group (-a is essential!)
groups bob                         # bob : bob developers
sudo useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin myapp
sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/deploy
#   deploy ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart myapp
sudo -u postgres psql              # run a command as another user
sudo passwd -l bob                 # lock the password
sudo userdel -r bob                # delete user and home directory
takeaways: usermod -aG adds a group; without -a you replace them all
Group changes apply at the next login
Edit sudo rules with visudo, in /etc/sudoers.d, allowing exact commands
pitfalls: `usermod -G developers bob` without -a, silently removing bob from sudo and every other group.

quiz.q: Why use visudo instead of editing /etc/sudoers with any editor?
options: It is the only editor root has
It checks the file for mistakes so an error can't break sudo
quiz.explain: A mistake in sudoers can make sudo unusable; visudo refuses to save a broken file.

quiz.q: You added alice to the developers group, but in her open terminal she still gets 'Permission denied' on the group's files. Why?
options: Groups are applied at login, so she must log in again or use newgrp
quiz.explain: A user's group list is set when they log in; new memberships show up in new logins.

concepts.name: Services with systemctl
concepts.summary: Start, stop, restart, reload, enable and inspect services with systemd's systemctl.
concepts.why: Nearly every server program runs as a systemd service, so systemctl is how you start, stop and check them.
concepts.body:
**systemd**, PID 1, starts and looks after **units**: the things it manages, each described by a small settings file, its **unit file**. The kind you'll use most is the **service** (`.service`): a program that should keep running in the background, such as nginx or PostgreSQL. Other kinds include timers (scheduled jobs), mounts, and targets: named groups of units, like `multi-user.target`, "everything a normal server runs".

You control them with `systemctl`:

- `systemctl status name` shows whether it's running, its main PID, its memory use and its latest log lines: the first command to run when something is wrong,
- `start`, `stop`, `restart`, and `reload` (reread its settings without a restart, if the program supports it),
- `enable` makes it start whenever the machine **boots** (starts up), `disable` undoes that; `enable --now` enables and starts it in one go,
- `is-active`, `is-enabled` and `is-failed` give short answers that suit scripts,
- `systemctl --failed` (or `list-units --state=failed`) lists units that broke,
- `systemctl cat name` shows the unit file, including any local changes; `systemctl show name` lists every setting.

Note the difference between **running now** (start/stop) and **starting at boot** (enable/disable). Forgetting to enable is a classic "it worked until the reboot" bug. `mask` stops a unit from being started at all.

Commands that change something need `sudo`. Users can also run their own services with `systemctl --user`. systemd collects everything a service prints into its log, the journal, which `journalctl -u name` reads (next lesson).
concepts.code:
systemctl status nginx              # state, PID, memory, recent log lines
sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl stop nginx
sudo systemctl restart nginx        # stop + start
sudo systemctl reload nginx         # reread settings, keep connections
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx   # start at boot AND right now
systemctl is-active nginx           # active
systemctl is-enabled nginx          # enabled
systemctl --failed                  # units that failed
systemctl cat nginx                 # the unit file and local changes
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running | head
systemctl --user status syncthing   # a service of your own user
takeaways: status first; start/stop/restart/reload for now, enable/disable for boot
enable --now does both
systemctl --failed shows what is broken
pitfalls: Starting a service but never enabling it, so it is gone after the next reboot.

quiz.q: Which command makes a service start at boot and also starts it immediately?
quiz.explain: enable sets it up to start at boot, and --now also starts it immediately.

quiz.q: What is `systemctl reload` for?
options: Rereading unit files after editing them
Telling the service to reread its settings without a full restart
quiz.explain: reload asks the program itself to reread its settings; daemon-reload is what rereads unit files.

concepts.name: Logs with journalctl
concepts.summary: Search the systemd journal by service, time, importance and boot, follow logs live, and keep its size in check.
concepts.why: When a service misbehaves, its logs are the first place to look, and journalctl finds them fast.
concepts.body:
systemd's **journal** collects in one place everything services print (their standard output and standard error), the kernel's own messages, and the messages of older-style logging tools. It stores them so they can be searched quickly. `journalctl` reads it, and its filters combine:

- `-u nginx` one service (repeat `-u` for several), `-k` kernel messages only,
- `-f` follow live, `-n 50` the last 50 entries, `-e` jump to the end,
- `--since "1 hour ago"`, `--since today`, `--until "2026-10-01 12:00"`,
- `-p err` only errors and worse. Each message has an importance level, from most to least urgent: `emerg`, `alert`, `crit`, `err`, `warning`, `notice`, `info`, `debug`,
- `-b` since this boot, `-b -1` the previous boot, `--list-boots` all of them,
- each entry also carries labelled details, such as `_PID=1234` or `_UID=1000`; match on them directly, and see them all with `-o json-pretty`.

Output opens in `less`; add `--no-pager` in scripts and pipe into `grep` as usual. Without `sudo` (or membership in the `adm` or `systemd-journal` group) you see only your own user's logs.

Whether logs survive a reboot depends on where they're kept. If the directory `/var/log/journal` exists, they're stored on disk; otherwise they live in `/run`, which is kept in RAM and emptied at every start. Size limits are set in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`; check usage with `--disk-usage` and trim with `--vacuum-size` or `--vacuum-time`.

Many programs (nginx, PostgreSQL) also, or instead, write classic text logs under `/var/log`, rotated by **logrotate**; read those with `less`, `tail -f` and `grep`.
concepts.code:
journalctl -u nginx                     # one service's logs
journalctl -u nginx -f                  # follow live
journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago" --no-pager | grep -i error
journalctl -p err -b                    # errors and worse, since this boot
journalctl -b -1 -e                     # previous boot, jump to the end
journalctl -k -n 20                     # last 20 kernel messages
journalctl _PID=1234                    # by one of the entry's details
journalctl -u nginx -o json-pretty -n 1 # every detail of one entry
journalctl --disk-usage
sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=2weeks    # drop older entries
sudo tail -F /var/log/nginx/error.log   # classic log files
takeaways: journalctl -u unit -f --since ... -p err -b: filter and follow
-b -1 reads the previous boot (if logs are kept on disk)
Many programs also write text logs in /var/log, rotated by logrotate
pitfalls: Looking for logs from before a crash and restart when the journal is only kept in RAM.

quiz.q: How do you see errors from the boot before the current one?
quiz.explain: -b -1 picks the previous boot and -p err keeps only errors and worse.

quiz.q: journalctl shows only a few lines for a system service when run without sudo. Why?
options: Ordinary users only see their own logs unless they're in adm or systemd-journal
The service prints to standard error
quiz.explain: System logs need root or membership in a log-reading group.

concepts.name: Scheduling: cron and systemd timers
concepts.summary: Run jobs on a schedule with cron or systemd timers, and avoid the surprises of cron's bare environment.
concepts.why: Nightly copies of important data, cleanups and reports all need to run reliably on a schedule, with nobody logged in.
concepts.body:
**cron** is the classic scheduler. Each **cron job** is one line: five time values, in the order minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week, followed by the command. `*` means every value, `*/5` every fifth, `1-5` a range, `1,15` a list. So `30 2 * * *` is 02:30 every day and `*/10 * * * 1-5` every ten minutes on weekdays. Edit your own list, the crontab, with `crontab -e` and show it with `crontab -l`; system-wide jobs go in `/etc/cron.d/`, with an extra value saying which user runs them.

Cron jobs run with a **bare environment**: a short `PATH`, none of your shell settings, and your home as the working directory. So use absolute paths, set the variables you need at the top of the crontab or in the script, and **redirect output** (`>> log 2>&1`), or it gets mailed to a mailbox nobody reads. Also, `%` has a special meaning in crontab lines and must be written `\%`.

**systemd timers** are the modern alternative: a `.timer` unit starts a `.service` unit on schedule. What you gain:

- output goes to the journal,
- `Persistent=true` runs a job that was missed while the machine was off,
- `RandomizedDelaySec=` spreads jobs out so they don't all start at once,
- the job gets everything a service gets, such as limits on memory use and start order,
- `systemctl list-timers` shows each timer's next and last run.

`OnCalendar=` takes schedules like `daily`, `Mon..Fri 09:00` or `*-*-* 02:30:00`; check when one fires with `systemd-analyze calendar`. For a single delayed command, `systemd-run --on-active=30m cmd` or `at` work.
concepts.code:
crontab -e                         # edit YOUR crontab, lines like:
#   m    h  dom mon dow  command
#   30   2  *   *   *    /home/ada/bin/backup.sh >> /home/ada/backup.log 2>&1
#   */10 *  *   *   1-5  /usr/local/bin/check-queue
crontab -l                         # list it
# systemd alternative: /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer
#   [Timer]
#   OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00
#   Persistent=true                # catch up if the machine was off
#   [Install]
#   WantedBy=timers.target
# ...plus backup.service with ExecStart=/home/ada/bin/backup.sh
sudo systemctl enable --now backup.timer
systemctl list-timers              # next and last run of every timer
systemd-analyze calendar 'Mon..Fri 09:00'   # when does this fire next?
takeaways: Five cron values: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week
Cron has a bare environment: use absolute paths and redirect output
systemd timers add journal logs, catch-up runs and list-timers
pitfalls: A script that works in your terminal but fails in cron because PATH or variables are missing.

quiz.q: What does the cron schedule `0 */6 * * *` mean?
quiz.explain: Minute 0, every sixth hour: 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00.

quiz.q: Which systemd timer option runs a missed job after the machine was powered off at the scheduled time?
quiz.explain: Persistent=true records the last run and triggers immediately if a run was missed.

concepts.name: How networks work: addresses, ports, DNS
concepts.summary: The ideas every network command assumes: IP addresses, network interfaces, routes, ports, TCP and UDP, and DNS names.
concepts.why: Network commands only make sense once you know what an address, a port and a name lookup are.
concepts.body:
When two computers talk, the data travels in small chunks called **packets**, each labelled with where it's going, like letters in the post. To deliver them, every machine on a network needs an address.

That address is the **IP address**: four numbers like `192.168.1.20` (IPv4), or a longer form with colons like `fe80::1` (IPv6). A machine connects to networks through **network interfaces**, such as a cable socket or Wi-Fi, and each one has its own address.

Every machine also has a pretend network interface, `lo`, with the address `127.0.0.1`, known as **localhost**. Traffic sent there never leaves the machine, so a program reachable only on localhost is invisible to the rest of the network.

Packets for other networks are handed to a **gateway**: a machine that passes traffic between networks, like a post office forwarding letters. Each machine keeps a **routing table**, a short list of rules saying where to send packets for which addresses. The rule for everything else, the default route, points at the gateway that leads to the internet.

One machine runs many network programs at once, so an address alone isn't enough. Each program uses a **port**, a number from 1 to 65535, like a flat number in a building: websites use 443 (and 80), SSH uses 22. A program waiting for connections on a port is said to **listen** on it. Listening on a port below 1024 needs administrator rights.

Most traffic follows one of two sets of rules. **TCP** first sets up a connection with a short exchange, the **handshake**, then makes sure everything arrives complete and in order. **UDP** just sends packets, with no connection and no guarantees; it's quicker. A program's end of a connection is called a **socket**.

People use names, not numbers. **DNS** is the internet's phone book: it turns a name like `example.com` into an IP address. A machine's own name is its **hostname**.

Finally, a **firewall** decides which packets may come in or go out, following rules like "allow port 443 from anywhere".
concepts.code:
hostname                      # web1   (this machine's name)
ip -br addr                   # network interfaces and their IP addresses
# lo    UNKNOWN  127.0.0.1/8 ::1/128
# eth0  UP       192.168.1.20/24
ip route                      # default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0   (the gateway)
getent hosts example.com      # <an IP address>  example.com   (a DNS lookup; the number varies)
cat /etc/resolv.conf          # nameserver ...   (which DNS server is asked)
grep -w 22 /etc/services      # ssh  22/tcp   (well-known port numbers)
head -n 3 /etc/hosts          # names listed by hand, checked before DNS
takeaways: An IP address finds the machine; a port finds the program on it
127.0.0.1 (localhost) never leaves the machine; the default route leads out
DNS turns names into IP addresses; TCP is reliable, UDP is quick
pitfalls: Blaming the network when the program simply isn't listening on the port you're trying.

quiz.q: A server runs both a website and SSH. What tells incoming traffic which program it's for?
quiz.explain: Both programs share the machine's IP address; the port number (443 or 22) picks the program.

quiz.q: What does DNS do?
options: Turns names like example.com into IP addresses
quiz.explain: DNS is the phone book of the internet: it looks up the IP address for a name.

concepts.name: Networking tools: ip, ss, dig, curl
concepts.summary: Inspect network interfaces, routes, listening ports and DNS, and test a connection step by step.
concepts.why: Most 'the service is down' problems are network questions you can answer with a handful of commands.
concepts.body:
When something on the network doesn't work, check it **step by step**, from the machine's own connection up to the program, and stop at the first step that fails:

- **Network interfaces and addresses**: `ip addr` (`ip -br a` for a short view) shows each network interface, whether it's up, and its IP addresses. The old `ifconfig` is outdated.
- **Routes**: `ip route` shows the routing table; the `default via` line names your gateway. `ip route get 8.8.8.8` tells which way packets to that address would go.
- **Reachability**: `ping -c 3 name` checks that a machine answers at all (some firewalls block ping); `tracepath` or `mtr` show each gateway on the way.
- **DNS**: `dig +short name` or `getent hosts name` (which also reads `/etc/hosts`). The DNS servers your machine asks are listed in `/etc/resolv.conf`, which often just points at systemd's local helper; `resolvectl status` shows the real ones.
- **Ports**: `ss -tlnp` lists the TCP ports programs are listening on, with each program's name (use `sudo` to see them all); `ss -tnp` shows open connections. A program listening on `127.0.0.1` can only be reached from the machine itself; `0.0.0.0` or `[::]` means every network interface.
- **The program**: `curl -v https://example.com/path` shows the whole exchange with a website: setting up the secure connection, what was asked, and what came back. `nc -zv name 5432` tests whether a TCP port accepts connections.

How the network is configured differs by distribution: netplan on Ubuntu, NetworkManager (`nmcli`) on Fedora/RHEL and desktops, systemd-networkd elsewhere.
concepts.code:
ip -br addr                   # network interfaces and their addresses
# lo    UNKNOWN  127.0.0.1/8 ::1/128
# eth0  UP       192.168.1.20/24 fe80::1c2:3ff:fe4d:5e6f/64
ip route                      # default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0 ...
ip route get 1.1.1.1          # which interface and own address would be used
ping -c 3 example.com         # does it answer, and how fast?
dig +short example.com        # just the DNS answer
getent hosts db.internal      # look a name up the way programs do (incl. /etc/hosts)
sudo ss -tlnp                 # listening TCP ports, with their programs
# LISTEN 0 511 0.0.0.0:80 0.0.0.0:* users:(("nginx",pid=812,fd=6))
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n' https://example.com
nc -zv db.internal 5432       # is that TCP port open?
takeaways: Check network interface, route, DNS, port, then the program
ss -tlnp shows what listens where; 127.0.0.1 means this machine only
dig / getent for DNS, curl -v and nc -zv for services
pitfalls: Concluding a machine is down because ping fails, when a firewall simply blocks ping.

quiz.q: A web app works with curl on the server but not from other machines. ss shows it listening on 127.0.0.1:8080. Why?
options: It listens only on 127.0.0.1, which other machines can't reach
quiz.explain: 127.0.0.1 accepts connections only from the machine itself; the program must listen on 0.0.0.0 or the machine's real address.

quiz.q: Which command shows listening TCP ports and the processes that own them?
quiz.explain: ss options: -t TCP, -l listening, -n show numbers, -p show the program.

concepts.name: Archives and compression: tar, gzip, zstd
concepts.summary: Bundle directories with tar, compress them with gzip, xz or zstd, and list or unpack archives safely.
concepts.why: Backups, software downloads and file transfers are almost always tar archives, nicknamed tarballs.
concepts.body:
**tar** packs files and directories, with their permissions and dates, into a single file, an **archive**; a compressor then shrinks it. The options read like a sentence:

- `c` create, `x` extract (unpack), `t` list the contents,
- `f file` the archive's file name (put it last in the group of letters),
- `z` gzip, `J` xz, `--zstd` zstd, or `a` to choose by the file name's ending,
- `v` verbose (name each file), `-C dir` change into a directory first.

So `tar -czf backup.tar.gz dir/` creates, `tar -tzf backup.tar.gz` lists, and `tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -C /restore` unpacks into a directory. Modern tar notices the compression by itself when unpacking, so `tar -xf` is usually enough. **List before unpacking** archives from elsewhere: some contain absolute paths, or a pile of files with no directory around them.

Compressors trade speed for size: **gzip** works everywhere, **xz** makes smaller files but is slow, and **zstd** is fast with good results and has become the default for many projects. Single files can be compressed directly: `gzip file` replaces it with `file.gz` (`-k` keeps the original), and `gunzip` or `zcat` reverse it.

`zip` and `unzip` handle the format common on Windows. To copy directories between machines, `rsync -a` or `tar` piped through `ssh` keep permissions, owners and dates.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)" # a fresh temporary directory mkdir -p site/css && echo '

hi

' > site/index.html && echo 'body{}' > site/css/a.css tar -czf site.tar.gz site/ # c=create z=gzip f=file tar -tzf site.tar.gz | sort # t=list: site/ site/css/ site/css/a.css site/index.html mkdir restore && tar -xf site.tar.gz -C restore # x=extract (compression detected) ls restore/site # css index.html tar -caf site.tar.xz site/ # -a: compression chosen from the name's ending echo 'log line' > app.log gzip app.log && ls app.log* # app.log.gz (original replaced) zcat app.log.gz # log line gunzip app.log.gz && ls app.log* # app.log # tar -cf - site/ | ssh backup 'tar -xf - -C /srv' # copy a tree to another machine
takeaways: tar -czf create, -tzf list, -xf extract, -C target directory
gzip works everywhere, zstd is fast, xz is small
List archives from elsewhere before unpacking them
pitfalls: Extracting an unknown archive in your home directory and getting hundreds of loose files.

quiz.q: Which command lists the contents of backup.tar.gz without extracting?
quiz.explain: t lists, x extracts, c creates.

quiz.q: What happens to app.log after `gzip app.log`?
options: It is kept next to app.log.gz
quiz.explain: gzip replaces the file with its compressed version unless -k is given.

concepts.name: Block devices, filesystems and mounts
concepts.summary: Find disks with lsblk, create file systems, mount them by UUID and make mounts permanent with fstab.
concepts.why: Adding a disk to a server, or rescuing one that won't start, requires understanding how disks become directories.
concepts.body:
Disks appear in `/dev` as **block devices**, device files read and written in fixed-size blocks: `/dev/sda`, `/dev/nvme0n1`, or `/dev/vdb` on a **virtual machine** (a computer simulated by software on a real one, as most cloud servers are).

A disk is usually divided into **partitions**, separate sections that are each used on their own, such as `/dev/sda1` or `/dev/nvme0n1p1`. `lsblk -f` shows the whole tree with file system types, labels, UUIDs and mount points; `blkid` prints the UUIDs.

A partition must hold a file system before use: `mkfs.ext4` or `mkfs.xfs` create one (and destroy whatever was there). **ext4** is the solid default; **XFS** is Red Hat's default and handles huge files well, but can't shrink; **Btrfs** can take **snapshots** (instant frozen copies of the whole file system) and keeps **checksums**, short fingerprints of the data that reveal corruption.

Mounting attaches a file system to a directory: `mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data`; `umount` detaches it. "target is busy" means some process still uses it (find it with `lsof` or `fuser -vm`). `findmnt` shows what is mounted where, with its options.

To mount at **boot** (each time the machine starts), add a line to `/etc/fstab`: device, mount point, type, options, and two numbers (`0` for the old dump tool, then the order for disk checks). Always name the device by **UUID**, a long random ID written into the file system when it's created, because names like `/dev/sdb` can change between boots. Useful options: `defaults`, `noatime`, `ro` (read-only), and **`nofail`** for disks the system can live without, so a missing one doesn't stop the start-up. Test with `findmnt --verify` and `mount -a` before rebooting: a broken fstab can leave the machine stuck in a bare repair mode.

Some file systems need no disk: `tmpfs` lives in RAM, and network file systems (NFS, SMB) mount folders shared by other machines.
concepts.code:
lsblk -f                            # disks, partitions, file systems, UUIDs, mount points
findmnt /                           # what is mounted at /, with options
sudo mkfs.ext4 -L data /dev/sdb1    # new file system (DESTROYS existing data)
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/data
sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data
sudo blkid /dev/sdb1                # UUID="3f1c..." TYPE="ext4" LABEL="data"
# /etc/fstab  (by UUID, never /dev/sdX):
# UUID=3f1c...  /mnt/data  ext4  defaults,noatime,nofail  0  2
sudo findmnt --verify               # check fstab before rebooting
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo mount -a   # mount everything listed
sudo umount /mnt/data               # "target is busy"? -> sudo fuser -vm /mnt/data
sudo mount -t tmpfs -o size=1G tmpfs /mnt/scratch   # a file system in RAM
takeaways: lsblk -f and blkid identify disks, file systems and UUIDs
mkfs creates a file system; mount attaches it to a directory
fstab by UUID with nofail; verify before rebooting
pitfalls: Using /dev/sdb1 in fstab, then a new disk shifts the names and the wrong device (or none) is mounted.

quiz.q: Why should /etc/fstab refer to filesystems by UUID?
options: Device names like /dev/sdb can change between boots
quiz.explain: The kernel names disks in the order it finds them; the UUID is stored inside the file system itself.

quiz.q: What does the `nofail` mount option do?
options: Makes the file system read-only on errors
Lets the system start even if that disk is missing
quiz.explain: Without nofail, a missing disk listed in fstab can stop the machine from starting normally.

concepts.name: Partitions and LVM
concepts.summary: Partition disks with GPT, and pool them with LVM to resize volumes online and take snapshots.
concepts.why: Growing a full disk while the server keeps running is routine but nerve-wracking, unless you know LVM.
concepts.body:
A disk's partitions are described by a **partition table** at its start. **GPT** is the modern standard (large disks, many partitions, needed by the UEFI start-up firmware of modern machines); the older **MBR** can't use more than 2 **terabytes** (about two thousand gigabytes) of a disk. Create partitions with `fdisk`, `gdisk` or the scriptable `parted`, then tell the kernel to reread the table (`partprobe`).

**LVM** (Logical Volume Manager) adds a flexible layer between disks and file systems:

- **physical volumes** (PV): disks or partitions prepared with `pvcreate`,
- a **volume group** (VG): a pool of space built from one or more PVs with `vgcreate`,
- **logical volumes** (LV): pretend block devices cut from the pool with `lvcreate`, used like partitions at `/dev/vgname/lvname`.

The payoff: when a volume fills up, add a disk to the VG (`vgextend`) and grow the LV **while it's mounted** with `lvextend -r`, where `-r` also grows the file system on it. ext4 and XFS can grow while mounted; only ext4 can shrink, and only unmounted. `pvs`, `vgs` and `lvs` summarise the layout.

LVM **snapshots** (`lvcreate -s`) freeze a view of a volume, handy before an upgrade or for a consistent copy. They use up space as the original changes, so remove them afterwards.

In the cloud you often grow the disk itself instead: resize it in the provider's console, then `growpart` the partition and grow the PV or file system. Always make a **backup**, a copy of the data kept somewhere else, before touching partition tables.
concepts.code:
sudo fdisk -l /dev/sdb                    # current partition table
sudo parted /dev/sdb --script mklabel gpt mkpart data 1MiB 100%
# LVM: physical volumes -> volume group -> logical volumes
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
sudo vgcreate vgdata /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
sudo lvcreate -n lvapp -L 50G vgdata
sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/vgdata/lvapp
sudo pvs; sudo vgs; sudo lvs              # summaries
# Out of space? Add a disk and grow online:
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdd1 && sudo vgextend vgdata /dev/sdd1
sudo lvextend -r -L +20G /dev/vgdata/lvapp   # -r grows the filesystem too
sudo lvcreate -s -n before-upgrade -L 5G /dev/vgdata/lvapp   # snapshot
# Cloud disk resized in the console instead:
sudo growpart /dev/nvme0n1 1 && sudo resize2fs /dev/nvme0n1p1   # (xfs_growfs for XFS)
takeaways: GPT partition tables; MBR only for old systems
LVM: PV -> VG -> LV, grow while mounted with lvextend -r
Snapshots before risky changes; remove them afterwards
pitfalls: Extending the logical volume but forgetting to grow the filesystem, so df shows no change.

quiz.q: You ran `lvextend -L +20G /dev/vg/lv` and df still shows the old size. What is missing?
options: Growing the filesystem (resize2fs / xfs_growfs, or use lvextend -r)
quiz.explain: The volume grew, but the file system on it has to be grown too.

quiz.q: What is a volume group in LVM?
options: A pool of storage made of physical volumes, from which logical volumes are allocated
quiz.explain: A VG pools PVs together; LVs are carved out of the VG.

concepts.name: /proc, /sys and sysctl
concepts.summary: Read process and system information straight from /proc and /sys, and change kernel settings with sysctl.
concepts.why: Tools like ps, top and free just read /proc; going there directly answers questions they can't.
concepts.body:
`/proc` is a virtual file system where the kernel publishes live information as text files. Nothing is stored on disk; each file's content is produced the moment you read it.

System-wide files: `/proc/cpuinfo`, `/proc/meminfo`, `/proc/loadavg`, `/proc/uptime`, `/proc/mounts`, `/proc/cmdline` (the settings the kernel was started with) and `/proc/pressure/*` (how much time programs spent waiting for the CPU, memory or the disk).

Each process has a directory `/proc/<PID>/`, and `/proc/self` is the one of whoever reads it:

- `cmdline` (its command, with the words separated by invisible zero characters), `environ` (its environment variables), and `cwd` and `exe`, links to the directory it works in and to its program file,
- `status` (state, memory use such as `VmRSS`, the user it runs as, and its number of **threads**: separate lines of work inside one process that run at the same time), `limits` (the most it may use of each resource),
- `fd/`: a program refers to each open file, pipe or network connection by a small number, a **file descriptor**; this directory has one link per descriptor,
- `cgroup` and `ns/`, covered in two Expert lessons.

`/sys` shows the hardware and the kernel's **drivers**, the parts of the kernel that operate each kind of device: network adapters in `/sys/class/net`, disks in `/sys/block`, CPU speed, power settings, and resource-limit groups in `/sys/fs/cgroup`.

**Kernel settings** live in `/proc/sys` and are managed with `sysctl`: `sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward` reads one, `sysctl -w` changes it until the next restart, and files in `/etc/sysctl.d/*.conf` make settings permanent (`sysctl --system` applies them).
