Common examples: `net.ipv4.ip_forward`, which lets the machine pass traffic between networks (machines that pass traffic between networks need it, and so does Docker); `vm.swappiness`, how readily memory is moved out to disk; `fs.inotify.max_user_watches`, how many files programs may watch for changes; and sizes of the memory set aside for network data in transit. Change settings deliberately and write down why.
concepts.code:
grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo
grep -E 'MemTotal|MemAvailable' /proc/meminfo
cat /proc/loadavg                       # 0.15 0.10 0.05 1/312 4567
tr '\0' ' ' < /proc/$$/cmdline; echo    # this shell's command line
readlink /proc/$$/cwd                   # the directory it works in
grep -E '^(State|VmRSS|Threads)' /proc/$$/status
ls -l /proc/$$/fd | tail -n +2 | head -n 3   # its open file descriptors
cat /sys/class/net/lo/mtu               # 65536
cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward       # 0 or 1, same as: sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
# sudo sysctl -w vm.swappiness=10                                  # until restart
# echo 'vm.swappiness = 10' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-local.conf # permanent
# sudo sysctl --system                                             # apply all files
takeaways: /proc/<PID>/ holds `cmdline`, `status`, `fd`, `cwd` and more for each process
/sys shows devices, drivers and resource-limit groups
sysctl -w for now, /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf for permanent
pitfalls: Changing a setting with sysctl -w and losing it at the next restart.

quiz.q: Where can you see every file and network connection a process with PID 812 has open?
quiz.explain: /proc/<PID>/fd holds one link per open file descriptor.

quiz.q: How do you make a sysctl setting survive reboots?
options: Write it to a file in /etc/sysctl.d/
quiz.explain: Files in /etc/sysctl.d are applied at every start; sysctl -w and writes to /proc/sys are lost at restart.

concepts.name: Firewalls: nftables, ufw and firewalld
concepts.summary: Filter incoming traffic with ufw or firewalld, and understand the nftables rules underneath.
concepts.why: A default-deny firewall that allows only the services you run is basic server hygiene.
concepts.body:
The kernel's own packet filter is called **netfilter**, and today it's configured with **nftables** (the `nft` command), which replaced the older iptables. On most systems the `iptables` command still exists, but only translates into nftables. Distributions add friendlier tools on top:

- **ufw** on Ubuntu: `ufw allow 443/tcp`, `ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 5432` (`10.0.0.0/8` means every address starting with 10.), `ufw enable`, `ufw status numbered`,
- **firewalld** on Fedora/RHEL: groups rules into **zones**, one per kind of network; `firewall-cmd --add-service=https --permanent` followed by `--reload`.

Use only one of these tools per machine; mixing them produces confusing, overlapping rules.

The usual policy for traffic coming **in** (nftables calls this list of rules the input chain): drop everything by default; accept packets that belong to connections already set up (**established/related**, such as replies to connections the server itself opened); accept the loopback interface `lo`; accept the ports you serve; and accept ICMP, the small control messages that ping uses. With IPv6, ICMPv6 is essential: machines use it to find each other on the local network.

Before switching on a drop-by-default policy over SSH, **allow SSH first**. Keep a second SSH connection open, or schedule an automatic **rollback** that undoes the change after a few minutes: locking yourself out of a faraway machine is a rite of passage best avoided.

Cloud companies add their own filters (security groups) in front of the machine, and Docker adds its own rules for the ports it publishes, which can bypass ufw. Check what's really active with `nft list ruleset`.
concepts.code:
# Ubuntu: ufw
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH            # FIRST, or you lock yourself out
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 5432 proto tcp
sudo ufw enable && sudo ufw status verbose
# Fedora / RHEL: firewalld
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=https --permanent && sudo firewall-cmd --reload
# nftables directly, /etc/nftables.conf:
# table inet filter {
#   chain input {
#     type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;
#     ct state established,related accept
#     iif lo accept
#     meta l4proto { icmp, ipv6-icmp } accept
#     tcp dport { 22, 443 } accept
#   }
# }
sudo nft -c -f /etc/nftables.conf && sudo nft -f /etc/nftables.conf   # check, then load
sudo nft list ruleset             # what is really active
takeaways: nftables is the kernel firewall; ufw and firewalld are friendlier tools on top
Default drop, allow established, loopback, ICMP and your ports
Allow SSH before enabling a firewall remotely
pitfalls: Enabling a default-deny firewall over SSH without allowing port 22 first.

quiz.q: Why does a server firewall accept `ct state established,related` packets?
options: So replies to connections the server opened (and existing connections) get through
It is required by ufw only
quiz.explain: The kernel tracks connections, so return traffic gets in without opening ports to new incoming connections.

quiz.q: Which statement about Docker and ufw is true?
options: Docker's own rules for published ports can bypass ufw
Docker requires ufw to be disabled
quiz.explain: Docker inserts rules that handle published ports before ufw's rules see the traffic.

concepts.name: Troubleshooting performance
concepts.summary: Diagnose a slow machine methodically: load, CPU, memory, swap, disk activity and the out-of-memory killer.
concepts.why: When a live system people depend on is slow, a calm checklist beats guessing and restarting things.
concepts.body:
Check resources one at a time. For each, ask three questions: how busy is it (**utilization**), is work waiting in line for it (**saturation**), and are there **errors**?

- **Load average** (`uptime`, `top`): the average number of processes running or waiting over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. On Linux it also counts processes waiting on the disk (state D), so compare it with `nproc` and check whether the CPU or the disk is the cause.
- **CPU**: `top` or `htop` per process; `mpstat -P ALL 1` per core. In the CPU figures, high `us` is time spent in programs, high `sy` in the kernel, and high `wa` waiting for **I/O** (input/output: reading and writing disks or the network). `st` (steal) matters on a **virtual machine**, a computer simulated in software as most cloud servers are: the real machine underneath is giving yours less CPU than you think.
- **Memory**: `free -h` (the available figure), `vmstat 1` with `si`/`so` for swapping. When memory runs out completely, the kernel's **OOM killer** (out of memory) ends a process to free some; `dmesg -T | grep -i oom` or `journalctl -k` show which.
- **Disk**: `iostat -xz 1` (from sysstat; install it with your package manager) shows per disk how busy it is, how much work is waiting, and the **latency** (`await`): how long each read or write took. `iotop` shows which processes use the disk; `df -h` rules out a full disk.
- **Per process**: `pidstat 1`, `/proc/<PID>/status`, and `lsof -p` for its open files and network connections.
- **Pressure stall information** in `/proc/pressure/{cpu,memory,io}` directly reports the share of time processes were stuck waiting.

`vmstat 1` is the best single first command: its `r`, `b`, `si/so` and `wa` figures show at a glance which resource is under pressure.
concepts.code:
uptime                      # load average: 3.10, 2.05, 1.20  (1, 5, 15 min)
nproc                       # 4 -> a load above 4 means processes are waiting
vmstat 1 5                  # r=running b=blocked si/so=swap wa=I/O wait st=steal
top -o %MEM                 # or htop; sort processes by memory
free -h                     # look at 'available'
cat /proc/pressure/memory   # some avg10=0.00 ... full avg10=0.00 ...
iostat -xz 1 3              # per-disk %util and await latency (sysstat)
sudo iotop -o               # processes using the disk right now
pidstat -u 1 5              # per-process CPU over time
sudo dmesg -T | grep -iE 'out of memory|killed process'   # OOM killer victims
sudo lsof -p 1234 | wc -l   # how many files and connections a process holds
takeaways: Check CPU, memory, disk and network for utilization, saturation and errors
vmstat 1 is the best first command; load counts disk waits too
dmesg / journalctl -k reveal OOM kills
pitfalls: Adding CPUs to a machine whose high load average is actually caused by tasks waiting on a slow disk.

quiz.q: A 4-core server has load average 12 but CPU is mostly idle and wa is high. What is the likely bottleneck?
quiz.explain: Linux load includes processes waiting on storage; an idle CPU with high wa points at the disk.

quiz.q: A process disappeared and the kernel log says 'Out of memory: Killed process 4242'. What happened?
options: The OOM killer ended it to free memory
quiz.explain: When memory runs out, the kernel's OOM killer picks a process and ends it.

concepts.name: Writing systemd unit files
concepts.summary: Turn your own program into a supervised service with a unit file: start order, restarts, user, settings and security limits.
concepts.why: A proper unit file gives your app automatic restarts, logs, start at boot and a security sandbox for free.
concepts.body:
Your own units go in `/etc/systemd/system/name.service`. A service unit has three sections:

- `[Unit]`: `Description=`, and when to start. `After=network-online.target` with `Wants=network-online.target` means "start once the network is up"; `Requires=postgresql.service` means "needs PostgreSQL running".
- `[Service]`: how to run it. `ExecStart=` needs an absolute path (one starting with `/`) and runs the program **directly**, not through a shell, so pipes and `$(...)` don't work unless you call `/bin/sh -c '...'`. `Type=simple` (the default: the program keeps running in the foreground), `notify` (the program tells systemd when it's ready) or `oneshot` (scripts that run and exit). Add `User=`, `WorkingDirectory=`, `Environment=` or `EnvironmentFile=`, and `Restart=on-failure` with `RestartSec=5`.
- `[Install]`: `WantedBy=multi-user.target` makes `enable` start it at boot.

After creating or editing a unit, run `systemctl daemon-reload`. To change a unit that came with installed software, don't edit it in `/usr/lib/systemd/system`. Run `systemctl edit name` instead: it creates a **drop-in**, a small extra file in `/etc/systemd/system/name.service.d/` whose settings take priority over the original's.

systemd can **sandbox** a service, fencing it in so it can only touch what it needs, with a few lines: `NoNewPrivileges=yes`, `ProtectSystem=strict` (the whole file system read-only except `ReadWritePaths=`), `ProtectHome=yes`, `PrivateTmp=yes`, or `DynamicUser=yes` for a throwaway user. `systemd-analyze security name` scores how exposed a service is. The app should just print its logs to standard output and standard error and let the journal store them.
concepts.code:
# /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service
[Unit]
Description=My web app
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=myapp
WorkingDirectory=/opt/myapp
EnvironmentFile=/etc/myapp/env
ExecStart=/opt/myapp/bin/server --port 8080
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/myapp
PrivateTmp=yes

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
# Then: sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now myapp
# Override a packaged unit instead of editing it: sudo systemctl edit nginx
takeaways: [Unit] when to start, [Service] how to run, [Install] start at boot
ExecStart runs without a shell; `daemon-reload` after edits
Use drop-ins via systemctl edit, and add sandboxing options
pitfalls: Writing `ExecStart=cd /opt/app && ./server`: there is no shell, so `cd` and `&&` don't work.

quiz.q: You edited /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service. What must you run before restarting it?
quiz.explain: daemon-reload makes systemd reread unit files; reload only asks the program to reread its own settings.

quiz.q: How should you customise a unit file installed by a package?
options: Create a drop-in with systemctl edit
quiz.explain: Drop-ins in /etc override just the settings you change, and survive software updates.

concepts.name: The boot process and kernel modules
concepts.summary: From power-on to login: firmware, bootloader, kernel, initramfs, systemd targets, and loading kernel modules.
concepts.why: Fixing a machine that won't start, or a device whose driver won't load, requires knowing each stage.
concepts.body:
Starting a machine happens in stages, each handing over to the next:

- **Firmware** (UEFI, or the older BIOS), built into the machine, checks the hardware and starts a bootloader from a small special **partition**, a separate section of the disk.
- The **bootloader** (GRUB, or systemd-boot) loads the kernel and the **initramfs** from `/boot`, and passes the **kernel command line**, the kernel's start-up settings (`/proc/cmdline` shows them afterwards), e.g. `root=UUID=... ro quiet`.
- The **kernel** sets up the devices and unpacks the initramfs: a small temporary root file system holding the drivers and tools needed to find the real one, for example on several disks combined into one, on a password-protected disk, or across the network.
- The initramfs mounts the real root file system and starts **systemd** as PID 1, which starts many units at the same time until the default **target** is reached (`multi-user.target` for servers, `graphical.target` for desktops).

`systemd-analyze`, `blame` and `critical-chain` show where start-up time goes. For rescue, edit the kernel command line in the bootloader menu and add `systemd.unit=rescue.target` or `emergency.target`.

Much of the kernel is built as **kernel modules**: pieces, such as drivers and file system types, that can be loaded into the running kernel when needed. They live in `/lib/modules/$(uname -r)`. `lsmod` lists the loaded ones, `modinfo` describes one, and `modprobe name` loads it together with the other kernel modules it needs (`-r` removes it). Kernel modules usually load by themselves when hardware appears. To load one at every start, list it in `/etc/modules-load.d/`; set its options, or block a driver you don't want, in `/etc/modprobe.d/`. After changes that affect the earliest stage of start-up, rebuild the initramfs (`update-initramfs -u` or `dracut -f`).
concepts.code:
systemd-analyze                     # Startup finished in 2.1s (kernel) + 6.4s (userspace)
systemd-analyze blame | head -n 5   # slowest units
systemd-analyze critical-chain      # what the boot actually waited for
cat /proc/cmdline                   # BOOT_IMAGE=/vmlinuz-6.12... root=UUID=... ro quiet
systemctl get-default               # multi-user.target
uname -r; ls /boot                  # running kernel vs installed kernels and initramfs
lsmod | head -n 5                   # loaded modules, sizes, users
modinfo -F description ext4         # Fourth Extended Filesystem
sudo modprobe br_netfilter          # load a module and its dependencies
echo br_netfilter | sudo tee /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf    # load at every boot
echo 'blacklist nouveau' | sudo tee /etc/modprobe.d/no-nouveau.conf
sudo update-initramfs -u            # Debian/Ubuntu (dracut -f on Fedora/RHEL)
takeaways: Firmware -> bootloader -> kernel + initramfs -> systemd -> default target
systemd-analyze blame / critical-chain explain slow start-ups
modprobe loads kernel modules; list them in `/etc/modules-load.d`, configure them in `/etc/modprobe.d`
pitfalls: Changing disk drivers, or setting up a password-protected disk, without rebuilding the initramfs, leaving a system that can't find its root file system.

quiz.q: What is the initramfs for?
options: A small early root file system with the drivers needed to mount the real one
quiz.explain: It lets a general-purpose kernel load support for the disks, LVM or encryption before the real root file system is available.

quiz.q: Which file shows the parameters the running kernel was booted with?
quiz.explain: /proc/cmdline shows exactly what the bootloader passed to the running kernel.

concepts.name: Namespaces: how containers isolate
concepts.summary: The private views Linux gives processes (process numbers, network, mounts, hostname, users and more), explored with unshare and nsenter.
concepts.why: Containers are just processes in namespaces; understanding them takes the mystery out of fixing Docker and Kubernetes problems.
concepts.body:
A **container**, the thing Docker runs, is an app with its own files, running sealed off from the rest of the machine, yet without a separate operating system. The main trick behind it is the **Linux namespace**: a wrapper around one kind of system resource, so the processes inside see their own private copy of it. Linux has eight kinds:

- **PID**: its own process numbering; the first process inside is PID 1,
- **network**: its own network interfaces, IP addresses, routing table, firewall rules and ports,
- **mount**: its own list of mounts, so a container sees its own root file system,
- **UTS**: its own hostname; **IPC**: its own channels for processes to pass messages to each other,
- **user**: its own mapping of UIDs and GIDs, so a process can be root inside and an ordinary user outside (the basis of "rootless" containers),
- `cgroup` and `time`: a private view of the groups Linux uses to limit resources (next lesson) and of some clocks.

Every process belongs to one namespace of each kind. `/proc/<PID>/ns/` shows them as links whose numbers identify each namespace, and `lsns` lists them all.

`unshare` starts a program in new namespaces (`--pid --fork --mount-proc`, `--net`, `--user --map-root-user`), and `nsenter -t PID -n` (or `-a` for all kinds) runs a command inside another process's namespaces. That's extremely useful with containers: you can use the machine's own tools, such as `ss`, `ip` or `tcpdump`, inside a container's network namespace, even if the container has none of them installed.

So a container is roughly: namespaces to keep it apart, resource limits (next lesson), its own root file system, and two features that take privileges away: **Linux capabilities** (root's powers split into separate pieces, so a process gets only the ones it needs) and **seccomp** filters (which block chosen system calls). There is no "container" as such inside the kernel.
concepts.code:
ls -l /proc/$$/ns | tail -n +2 | head -n 3   # cgroup, ipc, mnt ... -> 'net:[4026531840]'
sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc ps -o pid,cmd
#   PID CMD
#     1 ps -o pid,cmd       <- new PID namespace: only this process, as PID 1
sudo unshare --net ip -br link              # lo DOWN   (an empty network stack)
unshare --user --map-root-user id -u        # 0  (root inside, no sudo needed)
sudo unshare --uts bash -c 'hostname sandbox; hostname'   # sandbox (host unchanged)
lsns -t net                                 # network namespaces in use
sudo ip netns add blue && sudo ip netns exec blue ip -br link   # lo DOWN
pid=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' web)
sudo nsenter -t "$pid" -n ss -tlnp          # host's ss inside the container's netns
takeaways: Namespaces give processes private PIDs, network, mounts, hostname, IPC, users, resource groups and time
unshare creates namespaces; nsenter joins a process's namespaces
A container = namespaces + resource limits + root file system + reduced privileges
pitfalls: Installing troubleshooting tools inside a running container instead of entering its namespaces with nsenter.

quiz.q: Which namespace lets an unprivileged user appear as root inside a container?
quiz.explain: The user namespace maps UID 0 inside to an ordinary UID outside.

quiz.q: How can you run the host's `ss` command inside a container's network namespace?
quiz.explain: nsenter -n joins the target process's network namespace while running the machine's own ss program.

concepts.name: cgroups v2: limiting resources
concepts.summary: Control groups put processes in a tree and limit their CPU, memory, disk use and process count; systemd and container tools rely on them.
concepts.why: Every memory limit in Docker or Kubernetes, and every systemd resource setting, is a cgroup setting underneath.
concepts.body:
**Control groups** (cgroups) organise processes into a tree, and measure and limit how much of each resource they use. Modern distributions use the single **cgroup v2** tree, mounted at `/sys/fs/cgroup`. Each cgroup is a directory, and you control it by reading and writing its files:

- `cgroup.procs` lists the PIDs in the group (write a PID here to move that process in),
- `memory.max` is a hard memory limit (go over it and the OOM killer acts inside the group), `memory.high` a softer limit where the group is slowed down, `memory.current` the usage now,
- `cpu.max` is an allowance and a period in microseconds: `50000 100000` means 50,000 of every 100,000, i.e. half a CPU; `cpu.weight` is a relative share instead,
- `io.max` caps how fast each disk may be read or written, and `pids.max` the number of processes, which stops a **fork bomb** (a program that keeps copying itself until the machine chokes),
- `memory.events`, `cpu.stat` and the `*.pressure` files give statistics.

Each resource has a **cgroup controller** (memory, cpu, io, pids) that must be switched on for child groups in `cgroup.subtree_control`, and in v2 processes may only sit in the bottom-most groups of the tree.

**systemd** owns the tree: slices (`system.slice`, `user.slice`), services, and `.scope` units (groups for processes started outside systemd, such as your login) are all cgroups. So the right way to limit a service is with unit settings such as `MemoryMax=`, `CPUQuota=`, `TasksMax=` and `IOWeight=` (in a drop-in), and `systemd-run -p MemoryMax=... cmd` for a one-off command. `systemd-cgls` shows the tree and `systemd-cgtop` live usage per group.

Container tools such as Docker create one cgroup per container: `docker run --memory 512m` simply writes `memory.max`. Inside a container, `/proc/self/cgroup` shows which group you're in, and programs should size themselves by the limits found there, not by the whole machine's memory.
concepts.code:
findmnt -t cgroup2                  # /sys/fs/cgroup  cgroup2  ...
cat /proc/self/cgroup               # 0::/user.slice/user-1000.slice/session-3.scope
systemd-cgls --no-pager | head      # tree of slices, services and scopes
systemd-cgtop                       # live CPU/memory per cgroup
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/nginx.service/memory.current
# Limit a service (sudo systemctl edit myapp):
#   [Service]
#   MemoryMax=512M
#   CPUQuota=50%
#   TasksMax=200
systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=200M -p CPUQuota=25% ./batch-job.sh
# The raw interface that systemd and container runtimes use:
sudo mkdir /sys/fs/cgroup/demo
echo 100M | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/memory.max
echo "50000 100000" | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cpu.max    # half a CPU
echo $$ | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cgroup.procs          # move this shell in
takeaways: cgroup v2 is a directory tree at /sys/fs/cgroup; you control it through its files
memory.max, cpu.max, io.max and pids.max set limits
Use systemd settings (MemoryMax=, CPUQuota=) rather than writing the files by hand
pitfalls: Inside a container, sizing a program's memory use, or how many processes it starts, from the whole machine's memory instead of the cgroup's memory.max.

quiz.q: What does writing `50000 100000` to cpu.max do?
options: Allows 50 ms of CPU per 100 ms period: half a CPU
quiz.explain: cpu.max is the allowance, then the period, in microseconds: 50 ms of CPU time in every 100 ms.

quiz.q: A container hits its memory limit. What usually happens?
options: The kernel OOM-kills a process inside that cgroup
quiz.explain: Going over memory.max sets off the OOM killer inside that cgroup.

concepts.name: System calls and tracing with strace
concepts.summary: See exactly what a program asks the kernel to do with strace, and when to reach for lsof, perf and eBPF tools.
concepts.why: When logs say nothing, watching a program's system calls reveals the missing file, the stuck connection or the permission problem.
concepts.body:
Programs can't touch files, the network or other processes themselves: they ask the kernel through **system calls** such as `openat`, `read`, `write`, `connect`, `execve`, `clone` and `mmap`. Watching those calls shows what a program really does, whatever language it's written in.

`strace` prints them as they happen:

- `strace cmd` shows every call with its arguments and its result, the **return value**; errors appear as `= -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)`,
- `-f` follows child processes and threads, `-p PID` attaches to a process that's already running,
- `-e trace=openat,connect`, or groups like `%file`, `%network`, `%process`, pick which calls to show,
- `-T` shows the time spent in each call, `-tt` the time of day, `-c` a summary table, `-o file` writes to a file, `-s 200` shows longer strings.

Classic uses: finding which settings file a program looks for (`ENOENT` on `openat`), seeing why it gets `EACCES` (permission denied), discovering which server a stuck program is waiting on (`connect`, `poll`), and following which commands a script runs (`-e trace=execve -f`).

strace works through **ptrace**, a kernel feature for pausing and inspecting another program, and it slows the program down a lot, so be careful on live servers. Related tools: `ltrace` shows calls into **libraries** (ready-made code a program loads), `lsof -p PID` its open files and connections, `/proc/PID/stack` and `wchan` where a blocked process waits inside the kernel, and `perf top` / `perf record` act as a **profiler**, measuring where CPU time goes. To watch a busy live system cheaply, **eBPF** tools such as **bpftrace** and the BCC collection (`opensnoop`, `execsnoop`, `tcpconnect`) see the same events across the whole machine.
concepts.code:
strace -c ls / > /dev/null          # summary: calls, errors and time per syscall
strace -e trace=openat,read cat /etc/hostname
# openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/hostname", O_RDONLY) = 3
# read(3, "web1\n", 131072)              = 5
strace -f -e trace=execve bash -c 'ls | wc -l' 2>&1 | grep execve   # every program run
strace -e trace=%file -o trace.txt ./app; grep ENOENT trace.txt    # missing files
sudo strace -p 1234 -f -T -e trace=%network   # attach: what is it waiting on?
sudo lsof -p 1234 -a -i             # its network sockets
sudo cat /proc/1234/stack           # kernel stack of a blocked task
sudo perf top                       # where CPU time goes, kernel and user space
sudo opensnoop-bpfcc                # eBPF: every open() system-wide, low overhead
takeaways: Everything a program does with the outside world is a system call
strace -f -e trace=... -p PID shows what fails or what it waits for
strace is heavy; prefer eBPF tools on busy live servers
pitfalls: Leaving strace attached to a busy process on a live server, slowing it down dramatically.

quiz.q: A program says 'config not found' without naming the path. How can strace help?
options: strace -e trace=%file shows openat calls failing with ENOENT and their paths
quiz.explain: The failing openat calls reveal exactly which paths the program tried.

quiz.q: Why are eBPF tools preferred over strace on busy production systems?
options: They have much lower overhead than ptrace-based tracing
strace does not work on servers
quiz.explain: strace stops the process on every traced call via ptrace; eBPF runs small programs in the kernel instead.
